ADVERSE POSSESSION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION OF THE POSSESSION HISTORY SUPPORTING A CLAIMED ADVERSE POSSESSION
Jordan Alex Lee ("Declarant") states the following regarding real property located at 123 Main St, San Francisco, CA 94103, described as Lot 12, Block 4, per map recorded in Book 10, Page 5 (the "Property"), also identified by Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789, provided for identification only and not as part of the Property's legal description, situated in San Francisco County County, California.

The record owner of the Property, as reflected in the county records known to Declarant, is Taylor Morgan.

Declarant's possession of the Property is described as having begun on January 1, 2019, and consists of the following acts of use, cultivation, improvement, or enclosure of the Property during the period of possession described in this declaration: enclosed by fence and used as a garden.

The following describes the property taxes levied and assessed on the Property, and their payment, during the period of possession described above: paid all property taxes assessed since 2019, as shown on county tax records.

This declaration is Declarant's own factual account of possession, use, and tax-payment history with respect to the Property. It states facts as recounted by Declarant; it does not itself determine whether those facts satisfy the elements of adverse possession under California law, and it does not itself transfer, convey, or adjudicate title to the Property. A determination of title, if sought, is made by a court, not by this document.

TWO STATUTORY PATHWAYS TO ADVERSE POSSESSION: UNDER COLOR OF TITLE, AND UNDER CLAIM OF RIGHT ALONE
California's Code of Civil Procedure sets out two distinct statutory pathways by which land may be "deemed to have been held adversely," both located in the same chapter governing the time for commencing actions to recover real property. The first pathway applies where a claimant's possession is founded upon a written instrument (such as a deed purporting to convey the property), a judgment, or a decree — commonly called possession "under color of title." That statute requires that the occupant, or those under whom the occupant claims, entered into possession "under claim of title, exclusive of other right," founding that claim on the written instrument, judgment, or decree, and that there has been continued occupation and possession of the property described in it, under that claim, for five years; the property so included is then "deemed to have been held adversely." The second pathway applies where the claimant's possession is not founded on any written instrument, judgment, or decree — possession under a bare "claim of right." That statute uses closely parallel language: where there has been actual continued occupation of land "under a claim of title, exclusive of any other right," the land actually occupied (and no other) is "deemed to have been held adversely." The recurring statutory phrase "claim of title, exclusive of other right" is the textual source of what is commonly called the claim-of-right or hostility element of adverse possession, and the statutes' own "held adversely" language is the source of the term "adverse possession" itself, even though neither statute uses the word "hostile."

THE MANNER OF POSSESSION REQUIRED: ENCLOSURE, CULTIVATION, AND RELATED STATUTORY TESTS
California's Code of Civil Procedure states, separately for each of the two statutory pathways to adverse possession, what specifically counts as land having been "possessed and occupied." For a claim founded upon a written instrument, judgment, or decree (possession under color of title), land is deemed possessed and occupied where it has been usually cultivated or improved; where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure; where, although not enclosed, it has been used for the supply of fuel or fencing timber for husbandry, for pasturage, or for the occupant's ordinary use; or, for a known farm or single lot partly improved, where the unimproved or unenclosed portion is deemed occupied for the same length of time as the improved portion, following the usual course and custom of the surrounding area. For a claim not founded on any written instrument (a bare claim of right), the statute is narrower: land is deemed possessed and occupied only where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure, or where it has been usually cultivated or improved. Both statutes describe concrete, physical manifestations of possession — enclosure, cultivation, or specified uses of unenclosed land — rather than using the phrase "open and notorious," which does not appear in either provision's text.

THE PROPERTY-TAX-PAYMENT REQUIREMENT, AND ITS CERTIFIED-RECORD PROOF MECHANISM
California's adverse possession statute states that in no case is adverse possession considered established, under any section of the Code of Civil Procedure, unless the land has been occupied and claimed continuously for five years, and the claimant, or the claimant's predecessors and grantors, timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes levied and assessed on the land during that same five-year period. The same statute states how that tax payment is to be proved: payment of those taxes by the claimant, or the claimant's predecessors and grantors, must be established by certified records of the county tax collector. This tax-payment requirement is stated in a provision captioned as applying to a claim not founded on a written instrument, but its own text states that no adverse possession is established "under the provision of any section of this code" absent the five-year continuous occupation and tax payment described — language broad enough to extend the tax-payment requirement to a claim proceeding under the separate color-of-title pathway as well, not only to the bare-claim-of-right pathway in which this provision itself appears.

THE FIVE-YEAR STATUTORY PERIOD FOR ADVERSE POSSESSION
California's Code of Civil Procedure states the five-year period governing adverse possession from two directions within the same statutory chapter. One statute bars the true owner's own remedy: no action for the recovery of real property, or its possession, can be maintained unless the plaintiff, or the plaintiff's ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property within five years before the action is commenced. A second, related statute states a presumption and its rebuttal: in an action to recover real property, a person establishing legal title is presumed to have been possessed of the property within the time required by law, and another person's occupation is deemed subordinate to that legal title — unless the property has been held and possessed adversely to the legal title for five years before the action is commenced. Read together with the separate statutes on the manner of possession and, where applicable, tax payment (addressed in other clauses of this document), these two provisions confirm that five years, not some other figure, is the statutory period applicable to adverse possession in California.

  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 321, California Code of Civil Procedure, presumption of the title holder's possession, rebutted by five years of adverse possession (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=321.)

This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's five-year adverse possession period — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' adverse possession statutes commonly use different periods, some considerably longer than California's.

ADVERSE POSSESSION IS UNAVAILABLE AGAINST PUBLICLY OWNED OR PUBLICLY DEDICATED LAND
California's Civil Code states the general rule that occupancy, for the period the Code of Civil Procedure prescribes as sufficient to bar an action for recovery of the property, confers a title by prescription that is sufficient against all persons — the general prescriptive-title consequence of the Code of Civil Procedure's adverse possession statutes described in other clauses of this document. The same statute then states an express, unqualified exception: no possession by any person, firm, or corporation, no matter how long continued, of any land, water, water right, easement, or other property dedicated to a public use by a public utility, or dedicated to or owned by the state or any public entity, shall ever ripen into any title, interest, or right against that owner. This exception is not limited by any time period of its own — the statute states that such possession "shall ever" fail to ripen into title, regardless of duration.

expectedJSON.body: California's Civil Code states the general rule that occupancy, for the period the Code of Civil Procedure prescribes as sufficient to bar an action for recovery of the property, confers a title by prescription that is sufficient against all persons — the general prescriptive-title consequence of the Code of Civil Procedure's adverse possession statutes described in other clauses of this document. The same statute then states an express, unqualified exception: no possession by any person, firm, or corporation, no matter how long continued, of any land, water, water right, easement, or other property dedicated to a public use by a public utility, or dedicated to or owned by the state or any public entity, shall ever ripen into any title, interest, or right against that owner. This exception is not limited by any time period of its own — the statute states that such possession "shall ever" fail to ripen into title, regardless of duration.

citations.quote: Occupancy for the period prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure as sufficient to bar any action for the recovery of the property confers a title thereto, denominated a title by prescription, which is sufficient against all, but no possession by any person, firm or corporation no matter how long continued of any land, water, water right, easement, or other property whatsoever dedicated to a public use by a public utility, or dedicated to or owned by the state or any public entity, shall ever ripen into any title, interest or right against the owner thereof.
